strategy_title: num_warps-only autotune halves block size, worsens occupancy
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune that sweeps only num_warps and num_stages—without exposing BLOCK_M/BLOCK_N/BLOCK_K as constexpr kernel arguments—caused the autotuner to select a smaller block size (128→64 threads), which halved waves_per_sm from 0.93 to 0.47 and cut achieved occupancy from 11.78% to 5.88%, increasing duration from 70.08µs to 96.77µs. Because tile sizes remained hardcoded constexprs inside the kernel body, registers/thread stayed pinned at the 255 hardware cap regardless of num_warps chosen; the smaller block simply meant fewer warps hiding latency. This confirms the pattern from iteration 1: when registers/thread is at the hardware cap (255) due to large hardcoded tile sizes, num_warps-only autotuning is strictly harmful—it cannot reduce register pressure and only reduces parallelism.
applicable_when: Never. This is a pure anti-pattern. Document only to prevent future iterations from repeating it.
do_not_apply_when: Always avoid num_warps-only autotune when registers/thread >= 128 and tile sizes (BLOCK_M/BLOCK_N/BLOCK_K) are hardcoded constexprs inside the kernel body. The autotuner cannot reduce register pressure without tile size control, and selecting smaller block sizes reduces waves_per_sm and occupancy without any compensating benefit.
framework_notes: In Triton, constexprs defined inside the kernel body are invisible to @triton.autotune. Only parameters declared as kernel function arguments with tl.constexpr annotation AND included in triton.Config dicts are tunable. The grid lambda must use META['BLOCK_M'] etc. when tile sizes are autotuned. Iteration 2 also changed USE_FAST_ACCUM from True to False and BLOCK_K from 64 to 32, but these did not help because the fundamental issue (tile sizes not exposed to autotuner) remained.

strategy_title: maxnreg cap causes register spill, increases instruction count
strategy_description: Adding maxnreg=128 to triton.Config entries successfully reduced registers/thread from 168 to 128 and improved theoretical occupancy from 18.75% to 25% (Block Limit Registers: 3→4), but achieved occupancy remained essentially unchanged (11.93%→11.89%) because waves_per_sm dropped from 0.62 to 0.47. More critically, the register cap forced spilling to local memory: executed instructions increased by 27% (18.46M→23.48M), a new MemoryCacheAccessPattern rule fired indicating only 1/32 bytes utilized per sector for local loads/stores (62.63% speedup potential wasted), and L2 Compression Input Sectors exploded from 252K to 2.09M. The net effect was a 38% duration increase (67.65µs→93.06µs). When a kernel's register pressure is driven by large hardcoded tile sizes (BLOCK_M=64, BLOCK_N=128, BLOCK_K=32), capping registers via maxnreg causes spilling that overwhelms any occupancy benefit — the spill traffic to local memory creates a new, worse bottleneck than the original bank conflict stalls.
applicable_when: Never apply maxnreg when the kernel's register pressure is driven by large tile sizes (BLOCK_M*BLOCK_N*BLOCK_K accumulator tiles). Document only to prevent future iterations from repeating this pattern.
do_not_apply_when: Do NOT apply maxnreg=128 (or any register cap below the natural register count) when: (1) tile sizes are large hardcoded constexprs (BLOCK_M=64, BLOCK_N=128, BLOCK_K=32 or larger) that require many live accumulator values; (2) the natural register count is 128-168 (moderate, not at 255 hardware cap); (3) waves_per_sm is already below 1.0 — capping registers will force local memory spilling (MemoryCacheAccessPattern rule fires, L2 sector count explodes), increasing instruction count by 20-30% and worsening duration despite theoretical occupancy gains.
framework_notes: In Triton, maxnreg is passed as a keyword argument to triton.Config(). When the compiler is forced below the natural register demand by large tile sizes, it spills to local memory (thread-private stack in L1/L2). This is visible as: (1) MemoryCacheAccessPattern NCU rule firing with 1/32 bytes utilized per sector for local loads/stores, (2) large increase in L2 Compression Input Sectors, (3) executed instruction count increase of 20%+. The occupancy improvement from maxnreg is real (theoretical 18.75%→25%) but achieved occupancy does not improve because the spill traffic creates new stalls that offset the latency-hiding benefit of additional warps.
